current_episode.title: The Fast Five: Putting the “real” in real-world assets

guest.bio_context: Matt Hamilton brings experience from the oil and gas industry, where he works on the producer side and evaluates various financing mechanisms for commodity projects. Kevin Hamilton has been in crypto since 2012, having navigated multiple bear and bull markets, giving him deep expertise in digital asset structures. Together, they founded EtherStrike to bridge the gap between in-ground commodity financing and blockchain tokenization.

context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the Single Source podcast featuring fund managers at the forefront of private markets. I'm joined today by Matt and Kevin Hamilton, co-founders of EtherStrike. EtherStrike is the platform that tokenizes in-ground commodities. Please explain how do you do that? How did this come about? Matt and I were talking about some of the challenges he has in his oil and gas role. And we were talking about my background in crypto and thought there's a real opportunity to tokenize in-ground commodities. So, when we say in-ground commodities, what we're talking about is an oil field that is literally in the ground or a gold mine that hasn't been mined out yet. So, we're talking about commodities that are actually still in-ground that need to be extracted in some way. And when we talk about tokenization, we say we put the real in real world assets. And that means we are actually tokenizing things that are in the ground, not piece of the paper like securities or money market funds, but actual commodities. Elaborate on that a little bit more. You mentioned a dynamic reserve resource unit, DRRU. So, what does that token actually represent? How does an investor realize value or returns over the life of a project? RDRU is a security token and it represents a one-to-one match with that in-ground commodity. So, whether that's a barrel of oil, an ounce of gold, a standard cubic foot of natural gas, it is a match for that. And it represents the net proceeds from that recoverable reserve. The biggest value driver in our tiering structure is for investors to come along early in the journey. It's very hard for investors to get exposure early in pre-production projects. So, that tier compression and really coming on the journey from a discovery to pre-production to production. And when they buy at a discount, a properly priced discount, and move up through the tiers, I mean, that's really a significant value driver. As an example, our first strike is Asphalt Bluff South, which is 20 million barrels of asphalt binder in Utah. And so, we are tokenizing that in a one-to-one ratio for each of those barrels. Of all the real-world assets being tokenized right now, EtherStrike has focused on evaluating non-producing natural resources. Why non-producing? Can you give me an example? Yeah, we chose non-producing because that's where we saw the biggest gap, really. I sit on the producer side and so I see various financing mechanisms that come across my desk. And there are ways to do it, but each of them has their various obstacles. Private equity wants control. Venture capital wants a quick exit. None of those really work for a commodity that's been discovered but has years until it's actually producing. So, we came up with this new strategy to really fill that structural gap for a long production cycle. And when we're talking about these tokenized type of commodity reserves, they fundamentally, they're different from a crypto asset. Kevin, you told me that when you talk about the risk profile, but why are they different? What protection do investors have to minimize that downside risk? I've been in crypto since 2012. So, I've been through bear markets, winners, bull markets, and these are fundamentally different than a traditional crypto network or utility token. One of the biggest differences is that the floor of a traditional token is zero. There is no true floor, whereas for our tokens, the Druze, the underlying asset is actually what the token represents. And so, the floor is the net asset value of the commodity in the ground. So, if we're tokenizing an oil reserve, your token is backed one-to-one with a barrel of oil in the ground, and that is the fundamental floor of our token. Matt, in terms of allocation for our LPs on our Apex Invest platform, if you're already exposed to traditional commodities or private energy, where does this position fit? Is it a substitute, a complement, or a different category entirely? It's certainly a complement, maybe

pending_qa.q: How does EtherStrike's DRRU fit within a portfolio already exposed to traditional commodities or private energy?
pending_qa.r: The DRRU is positioned as a complement — and potentially a distinct category — relative to futures-based commodity ETFs or private energy plays. Compared to a commodity ETF, it offers direct exposure to a specific asset without additional roll costs; compared to private energy, it offers a leaner fee structure and secondary market liquidity. The closest existing analogy is a royalty trust, which similarly provides fractional ownership of production proceeds without equity in the operating company.
